title: BIA Overrules 14-Year Advance Parole Precedent, Putting DACA Green Card Pathway at Risk
excerpt: The Board of Immigration Appeals ruled that travel on advance parole now counts as a statutory departure, potentially triggering 10-year bars for DACA recipients and TPS holders with unlawful presence.
body:
• The Board of Immigration Appeals overruled the 14-year-old Arrabally precedent, ruling that travel on advance parole now constitutes a statutory "departure" that can trigger unlawful presence bars.
  • DACA recipients and TPS holders with one or more years of unlawful presence who travel on advance parole after August 13, 2026 may face a 10-year bar to re-admission.
  • The ruling applies prospectively — individuals who relied on the prior rule for past travel are not retroactively penalized.
  • Immigration attorneys are urging affected individuals to consult legal counsel immediately before any international travel on advance parole.

The Board of Immigration Appeals issued a precedent decision on August 13 that fundamentally changes how immigration authorities view travel on advance parole, overruling a 14-year-old ruling that had served as a critical pathway to green cards for DACA recipients and other immigrants with accrued unlawful presence.

In Matter of Delcarmen-Lara (29 I&N Dec. 830), a three-judge BIA panel held that departing the United States under advance parole constitutes a "departure" under Section 212(a)(9)(B) of the Immigration and Nationality Act. The ruling expressly overrules Matter of Arrabally and Yerrabelly (25 I&N Dec. 771, BIA 2012), which had held that advance parole travel was not a statutory departure for purposes of triggering the three-year and 10-year unlawful presence bars.

What Changed and Why It Matters

Under the Arrabally rule, immigrants who had accumulated unlawful presence could travel abroad on advance parole and return without triggering the bars to admissibility. This protection allowed thousands of DACA recipients who entered the country without inspection to use advance parole, adjust status through a U.S. citizen spouse or family member, and obtain green cards without needing a waiver.

https://x.com/Fernand46357857/status/2093482092906627499

The BIA's new interpretation eliminates that protection. The Board concluded that the statutory definition of "departure" contains no exception for parole-authorized travel. Because Congress included advance parole exceptions in other parts of the INA but wrote no such exception into Section 212(a)(9)(B), the Board applied the interpretive canon from Russello v. United States: the omission was deliberate, not an oversight.

"A harsh result is not the same as an absurd one, and Congress — not the Board — sets that policy."

— Board of Immigration Appeals, citing Cheruku v. Attorney General

Anyone with one year or more of unlawful presence who departs on advance parole after August 13 can now trigger the 10-year bar to admissibility. Those with 180 days to one year risk the three-year bar. To overcome the bar, individuals would need an I-601 waiver, which generally requires demonstrating extreme hardship to a U.S. citizen or lawful permanent resident spouse or parent — a U.S. citizen child does not qualify as a qualifying relative.

Prospective Application Offers Some Protection

The BIA determined that the new rule applies prospectively. Travel on advance parole completed before August 13, 2026 will not trigger the unlawful presence bars under this interpretation. The Board applied a multi-factor retroactivity test from Matter of Cordero-Garcia, concluding that the rule represents an abrupt shift from established practice, that immigrants heavily relied on the prior precedent, and that retroactive application would impose an undue burden.

However, the prospective protection has limits. Immigration attorney Joseph Tsang cautioned that individuals who have approved advance parole but have not yet traveled face the new rule squarely. "If you have advance parole and haven't left the country yet, or you're weighing whether to travel, this isn't a decision to make on your own," he said. "Talk to an immigration attorney before you leave, even if your advance parole was approved before August 13."

Who Is Affected

The ruling impacts several categories of immigrants. DACA recipients who entered without inspection and planned to use advance parole to adjust status through a family petition face the most direct consequences. TPS holders with accrued unlawful presence and pending adjustment-of-status applicants are also affected.

Immigration law firm Goel & Anderson advised employers to identify sponsored employees with pending adjustment applications or TPS-based advance parole who have accrued more than 180 days of unlawful presence, and to suspend planned advance parole travel for affected individuals until legal counsel has reviewed each case.

Legal Challenges Expected

Delcarmen-Lara is a precedential BIA decision binding on immigration judges and USCIS adjudicators nationwide unless reversed by a federal circuit court or the BIA itself. Given the 14 years of contrary guidance and the reliance interests built up during that time, attorneys say a circuit court challenge is plausible and would likely focus on whether the BIA's new statutory reading is entitled to judicial deference.

The Murthy Law Firm noted that individuals with prior unlawful presence "may become inadmissible under INA § 212(a)(9)(B) because of travel on advance parole, and may need a waiver before being able to obtain permanent residence or otherwise be admitted."

What Comes Next

Immigration practitioners are advising immediate caution. Anyone with accrued unlawful presence should consult an attorney before international travel on advance parole. Employers should route all advance parole travel requests through immigration counsel before departure is booked. The legal community is watching for a federal circuit court challenge that could test whether the BIA's reversal of such a long-standing precedent will survive appellate review.
